newsitem.title: UK: Cheap fridges to cool energy use by Britain's poor.
newsitem.headline: Cheap fridges to cool energy use by Britain's poor.

text.p: Britain's poor are to be sold 25,000 subsidised fridges in a scheme combining energy efficiency, environmental protection and social assistance, officials from the Energy Saving Trust said on Tuesday.

Low income families will trade in old inefficient fridges and pay 25 pounds for a new Turkish-made unit, saving some 100 pounds ($150) on retail prices and at least 30 pounds ($45) a year on electricity costs.
"The vast majority of people will save more than the purchase cost in the first year and get a nice new fridge into the bargain," EST programme manager Alex Goodwin said.
The innovative programme has no precedent in Britain though Goodwin said he believed it had been tried in the United States.
The 2.5 million pound national campaign is backed by funds from Britain's 14 electricity supply companies as part of their attempts to meet regulatory targets for promoting energy efficiency.
"Research shows that low income groups use products that consume more energy because their appliances tend to be older and broken," said Goodwin. "The pilot schemes have gone down extremely well."
Over the 15-year average lifetime of the new fridge each household should save 450 pounds, Goodwin said.
The old fridges will have their CFC gases safely removed and the environment will also benefit by energy savings that should mean 95,000 tonnes less carbon dioxide pumped into the atmosphere.
The EST, a non-profit company, has administered other energy-saving schemes for the electricity companies and for the British government.
It spent 18 million pounds promoting the use of low-energy light bulbs in Britain through publicity and subsidies until they became widely accepted.
The electricity companies spend some 25 million pounds a year promoting energy efficiency through the equivalent of a one pound levy on the bill of every power user.
"But that one pound a year returns about five pounds a year in energy saved, so it is quite efficient," Goodwin said.
